articles.title: Attackers backdoor trusted AWS integrations to steal secrets
articles.text:
Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship.

Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments.

“Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions.

Neither AWS nor Qubole responded to The Register's inquiries.

Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles.

The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872, and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS, Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote.

This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account.

Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store.

The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments.

Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data.

The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data.

While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity.

Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued.

Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses.

“For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.”®

articles.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
articles.text:
Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting.

The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.

Attackers conducting "mature intrusions"

Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.

articles.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
articles.text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. 

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport. 

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. 

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. 

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.title: Netting To Shield F-35s At Tyndall AFB From Drone Attacks Eyed By USAF
articles.text:
The U.S. Air Force is looking for contractors who could install netting at Tyndall Air Force Base in Florida to help protect F-35 Joint Strike Fighters from drone attacks. The netting plan, which has yet to be finalized, does reflect growing support for increased physical hardening of bases within the U.S. military, especially against uncrewed aerial threats. At the same time, it also calls attention to how the Air Force, in particular, has dragged its feet, if not actively pushed back, on such efforts.

The Air Force’s 325th Contracting Squadron at Tyndall announced last Friday that it was conducting “market research to identify qualified sources capable of providing all design, materials, labor, and equipment necessary to furnish and install counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS) netting” around six sunshade-type shelters at the base. Each one of these open-ended structures is 630 feet long, 65 feet wide, and 30 feet high. They are designed to accommodate up to six F-35As apiece at a time.

Today, Tyndall is a major hub for Air Force F-35 operations. Situated on the Florida Panhandle with ready access to extensive ranges in the Gulf, it is also an important facility for training and other activities. The base notably hosts the Checkered Flag large-force exercise series, which regularly includes participants from elsewhere across the U.S. military, as well as foreign allies and partners.

It is important to note here that the six structures mentioned in the notice only reflect a portion of the sunshade-type shelters at Tyndall. F-35s and other aircraft, including ones visiting for exercises and other training, also regularly park out in the open along the base’s flightline.

At this time, “the Government does not guarantee that a contract will result from this notice, and the Government will not reimburse any costs incurred by interested parties in preparing or submitting a response,” the contracting notice stresses. It does, however, lay out key parameters.

The 325th Contracting Squadron’s notice says the prospective counter-drone “netting installed on the north- and south-facing sides shall be quickly and easily retractable to allow normal aircraft entry and exit.” It has to have a tensile strength of at least 200 pounds and a mesh with squares no more than three inches across. Overall, the nets have to be “capable of stopping Group 1 small UAVs from penetrating the structure without compromising the netting.”

The U.S. military breaks drones down into five tiers, with Group 1 being the lowest. It covers designs with maximum takeoff weights of 20 pounds or less, that can’t fly above altitudes of 1,200 feet, and have maximum speeds of no more than 100 knots. Quadcopter-type drones, including weaponized commercial types, are a prime example of what falls into the Group 1 category. There are also fixed-wing uncrewed aerial systems that meet those parameters.

Beyond their counter-drone capabilities, the nets would have to be “UV-resistant, moisture-resistant, capable of withstanding temperatures up to 400°F,” and “polyester or nylon are preferred.” They also “must meet Miami-Dade County Wind Load rating requirements.” These requirements are in line with Tyndall’s location in the Florida Panhandle, where hurricanes and other extreme weather are also real concerns.

Drone threats to aircraft parked in the open are not new

TWZ has been sounding the alarm on threats posed by drones, small and large, to aircraft sitting out in the open for more than a decade now. Ukraine’s unprecedented Operation Spiderweb attack last year thrust these threats fully into the public consciousness. Spiderweb involved coordinated localized covert attacks on airbases across Russia using large waves of weaponized quadcopter drones. At least 10 Russian bombers, as well as a variety of other aircraft, all sitting on open flightlines, were destroyed.

Even before Operation Spiderweb, the U.S. Air Force had at least considered installing nets or other physical barriers to help blunt drone attacks on parked aircraft at Langley Air Force Base in Virginia and Seymour Johnson Air Force Base in North Carolina.

The potential plans to erect netting around sunshade-type shelters for F-22 Raptor fighters at Langley notably followed still largely unexplained drone incursions over that base in December 2023, which TWZ was the first to report. The Langley incursions reflected years of worrisome trends we had already been reporting on regarding the threat of drone attacks to key U.S. military bases and critical infrastructure within the U.S. homeland, as well as in waters just off America’s coastlines.

The scale and scope of potential drone threats on and off conventional battlefields has only continued to grow since. Just earlier this year, amid major combat operations against Iran, there were new reports of unauthorized drones flying over Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, a major Air Force bomber hub, and other strategic military facilities in the United States. A similar surge in drone incidents at key bases hosting U.S. forces, as well as commercial airports, in Europe has also been documented.

In October, the Air Force made a sudden and unexpected decision to withdraw B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford, an airbase in the United Kingdom. Still, unconfirmed reports said that the move was driven by concerns about an Iranian-directed drone attack broadly akin to Operation Spiderweb.

Separate from any particular mode of attack, the vulnerability of aircraft parked out on open flightlines is well established at this point, in general. This point was driven home for the U.S. military more directly by an Iranian missile and drone barrage on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia in March, which destroyed a prized E-3 Sentry Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) radar plane and damaged several KC-135 tankers. F-15E Strike Eagles and A-10 Warthog ground attack jets were also reportedly damaged following Iran’s attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan in September.

Counter-drone nets would not have stopped the attacks on Prince Sultan or Muwaffaq Salti, in which both included ballistic missiles. Iran also launched long-range kamikaze drones much larger and more capable than any Group 1 design at Prince Sultan Air Base.

In March, Iranian-backed militias in Iraq also launched localized drone attacks on a U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter and other American assets in that country, where nets could have offered additional protection.

A matter of urgency

Despite the years of concerning drone incursions, as well as observations from the conflict in Ukraine and now the experiences from the war with Iran, the Air Force has continued to, at best, downplay the value of physical hardening of infrastructure. A debate surrounding the pros and cons of building new hardened aircraft shelters has become a particular flashpoint. More recently, the service’s top leader has voiced support for nets and other lower-cost passive defenses, while still pushing back on shelters.

“There is value in some light protection against small, unmanned threats,” Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told Breaking Defense in July. “Some of them — just nets that are up that keep a small, few-$100 drone from getting next to a $2 billion aircraft. That actually works, [and is] really cheap.”

Otherwise, “I think that I don’t want to spend a lot of money on hardening shelters. Unless you’re going to send something 100 feet or more underground, we can blow it up, and so can they,” Wilsbach said in the same interview. “So, the economics of building a shelter that is impervious to a strike doesn’t work.”

“I think the economics favor defending your airspace, defending your ground space with systems that can defeat the incoming rounds, versus building a shelter,” he added. “Some people would argue, well, you should do both. Well, that’s even more expensive. And the other thing is, the shelter doesn’t go anywhere.”

Wilsbach’s comments here came in response to a direct question about whether he still stood behind similar remarks he made back in 2023. At that time, he was head of Pacific Air Forces (PACAF), the Air Force’s top command in that region. In recent years, other Air Force officers have similarly downplayed calls for construction of new hardened aircraft shelters, in particular.

When it comes to base defense and reducing vulnerability of aircraft on the ground, the Air Force has focused more on active measures like traditional surface-to-air missile batteries and anti-aircraft guns, as well as directed energy weapons and electronic warfare systems. The service also continues to put heavy emphasis on dispersal and deception, as well as new and still-evolving distributed concepts of operations.

As TWZ has reported on several occasions now, the key counterpoint when it comes to shelters, at least, is that not all such structures have to be stereotypical Cold War-era concrete bunkers to be useful. Just like nets can provide a valuable additional lower-cost layer of counter-drone protection, less-well-protected shelters that are cheaper to build would still offer benefits.

As we have written in the past:

“A structure that shields against smaller blasts and shrapnel, also including from cluster munitions that can be readily scattered across wide areas, is one that then has to be addressed by more capable weapons. This could even include mobile or otherwise temporary shelters that offer sufficient concealment and protection.”

“Eliminating, or at least substantially mitigating, the lowest rung of threats creates a dilemma for opponents, who then have to decide whether it is even worthwhile to attempt certain types of attacks. There is clear value in narrowing the available options for the enemy and pushing them toward having to expend higher-end, more expensive munitions, that are available in smaller quantities, and that traditional active defenses may be better optimized to handle. As an example, it may be more viable to shoot down a small barrage of incoming cruise missiles than a swarm of dozens of drones.”

Fully enclosed shelters, even ones that aren’t hardened, can offer additional benefits beyond protecting against hostile attacks. As mentioned earlier, extreme weather is a real threat to aircraft parked out on open flightlines, too. Tyndall Air Force Base in Florida is an especially notable case study to consider in this regard.

In 2018, Hurricane Michael ravaged Tyndall. At the time, the base was home to a significant portion of the Air Force’s highly prized F-22 fleet. Approximately 17 F-22s had to ride out the storm in existing hangars, and four sustained significant damage. As the scope of required repairs to Tyndall’s infrastructure became clear, F-22 operations there came to an end. Jets from the base were reassigned permanently to other units around the country. The Air Force only formalized plans to turn the Florida base into a new hub for the F-35 in 2021, and the first Joint Strike Fighters began arriving there in 2023.

Trends at home and abroad

TWZ has long highlighted how the Air Force’s position on the construction of new shelters bucks very visible trends elsewhere globally, including in China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran. Even before Operation Spiderweb, expanding Ukrainian drone and missile attacks had pushed Russia to begin building new and increasingly large hardened shelters at various bases, especially on the occupied Crimean Peninsula.

For years now, counter-drone netting, as well as cage-type armor, has also been increasingly in use in Ukraine and Russia for protecting static structures and fighting positions, as well as vehicles on land and ships at sea. These are other trends that have been expanding globally, as well.

As highlighted by Gen. Wilsbach’s comments to Breaking Defense in July, the U.S. military has clearly been taking notice of global developments when it comes to aspects of physical hardening. At the end of January, the Pentagon, by way of Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401), also notably issued new guidance for protecting critical infrastructure against drone attacks that explicitly called for increased use of netting, along with cables and other kinds of passive physical defenses. JIATF-401 was established in late 2025 to serve as a focal point for counter-drone efforts across the U.S. military, as well as other branches of government, and to help accelerate the fielding of new capabilities.

The counter-drone guidance the Pentagon promulgated earlier this year did also make clear that there is no one single solution to threats posed by uncrewed aerial attackers. Nets and other passive measures are complements, not substitutes for active defenses and other relevant tactics, techniques, and procedures. By the same token, however, they are valuable, if not increasingly critical, additions to a comprehensive layered defensive architecture.

“The technology is not going to solve this problem for us. We can’t field a system that will stop every drone,” U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, Director, head of JIATF-401, told TWZ and other outlets during a press call in December 2025 in response to a direct question about physical hardening from this author. “At the end of that would be protection, which would be netting or fencing or physical barriers that would prevent a [sic] unmanned system from having its intended effect.”

As it stands now, prospective contractors have until November 13 to submit details about how they would go about installing counter-drone netting at Tyndall if and when the Air Force decides to move ahead with that project. In the meantime, the contracting announcement only reinforces the continued and increasingly glaring lack of urgency with which the service is pursuing any kind of physical hardening.

articles.title: Researchers pwn automakers’ Android apps to remotely unlock cars, honk horns
articles.text:
Security researchers exploited flaws in Android apps to gain remote access to connected cars from two major automakers, allowing them to start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns.

Shubham Shah, co-founder at Assetnote, and researcher Sam Curry worked together on the exploits earlier this year. By tinkering with the cars’ Android apps, they devised exploit paths to issue remote commands to vehicles in Australia and the US.

The pair published separate blogs covering different aspects of the research; Shah said the US attack "required a lot more work" because the automaker "spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments."

Both exploit chains centered around weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity platform relied upon by both automakers, the identities of which were kept anonymous by the researchers, who have previously highlighted flaws in the likes of Hyundai, Kia, Subaru, and many others.

In the Australian version of the app, the researchers first found a vehicle identification number (VIN) using public licence plate checkers, and used those in queries to internal APIs, which provided personal information and owner email addresses.

They also found hardcoded admin credentials for the ForgeRock OpenIDM that were meant for the staging environment but also worked in production. After bypassing the heavy WAF filtering by exploiting path traversal flaws, they were able to invoke the internal admin APIs and take over target accounts using only their email addresses.

This let them mint authentication tokens, which they could issue to send arbitrary commands to affected vehicles through the mobile app.

Issuing commands on the US version also required bypassing WAF filtering through a path traversal, though with a more involved technique: exploiting path confusion to reach the Apache Felix admin console.

The researchers used factory default credentials in Felix’s OSGi Web Console to gain admin privileges. They then used Felix configuration manager to schedule a task that executed an inline Groovy script, giving them shell access to the identity servers.

The researchers then queried local admin API endpoints, allowing them to view or modify user account data. From there, they logged into car owners’ accounts, and gained the ability to issue the same commands as demonstrated in the Australian version.

According to Curry’s disclosure timeline, he and Shah approached the affected automakers in "early 2026," and the exploits were patched within two hours of receiving the report.

Although the automakers wished to remain anonymous, it didn’t take long for some petrolheads to speculate that the partially blurred car in Shah’s demo video was a Toyota, citing the shape of the wing mirror and the unlock sound it made.

Onlookers claimed that the two automakers in question were likely Toyota and its luxury brand Lexus. Asked wether the claims were accurate, a spokesperson for Toyota Motor Corporation neither confirmed nor denied them.

Curry said he and Shah chose to uphold the manufacturers’ requests to remain anonymous out of concern for infoseccers’ current workloads.

He said: "Obviously, they have asked not to be named, and while normally we would fight to actually include the company names, it's a busy time in the security world and I don't like the idea of them diverting resources because they are worried about something with this disclosure." ®

articles.title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
articles.text:
Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.

The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ".claude/settings.local.json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.

This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.

articles.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
articles.text:
As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. 

I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. 

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. 

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. 

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

Insight about how 'nature makes no leaps' promises better robot predictions
articles.text:
Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave.

World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes.

Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus."

The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom "nature makes no leaps," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference.

Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time."

Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models, developed by LeCun and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action.

But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to anticipate counterfactual scenarios – events that didn't happen. The technique that the researchers developed is not specific to JEPAs – it can be applied to any world model that predicts the average next state under any action. But JEPA models are particularly well suited to being adapted.

Balestriero said that the counterfactual world model experiments were done using off-the-shelf encoders (DINOv2 and MAE) without any fine-tuning and only a small predictor trained on top. Creating a counterfactual world model from that starting point would only require minor additions.

Counterfactual world models predict alternative scenarios more effectively by inferring possibilities from what did occur.

"In causal inference, answering 'What would have happened had I acted differently?' takes three steps," explained Balestriero. "You use what you observed to learn something about those hidden factors, you change the action, and you predict again with the hidden factors kept exactly as they were.

"Our counterfactual world model does all three steps with one subtraction."

Balestriero cited an example from the paper: a boat crossing a river with a hidden current and how the JEPA world model and counterfactual world model predicted the boat's movements.

"The world model predicted where the boat would end up after steering left, and it actually ended up two meters further downstream," he explained. "Those two meters are the signature of the current that occurred. To answer 'where would the boat be had I steered right?', we take the world model's prediction for steering right and add the same two meters. In other words, the counterfactual is what actually happened, plus the difference between the model's predictions for the alternative action and for the action taken.

"Physics enters to justify this rule, not as an equation the model fits. Over a short time, the effect of the action and the effect of the current each grow in proportion to the duration, while their interaction grows only with its square, so over short steps they simply add up, like forces.

"We prove that the fraction of the disturbance's effect that this rule gets wrong shrinks with the square of the time step, and that no method using the same ordinary data can do better than this rate in the worst case."

Counterfactual world models have three likely uses, according to Balestriero. The first is having a robot retry an action after a surprise event.

"When an attempt fails because of something the robot could not see, such as an unexpected load, a current or a weak motor, the counterfactual world model lets it estimate which action would have worked in that same situation," he explained. "In our simulated tasks, choosing the action this way reaches the goal in 35 to 69 percent of events, against 14 to 23 percent for a planner that knows the true simulator but ignores the observed outcome. With two more attempts on the same event, success rises to 51 to 97 percent."

He also sees these models being useful for adapting to persistent fault, like a miscalibrated motor, and helping people understand failures.

"World models are trained to predict, and they are getting good at it," said Balestriero. "But a robot, a car or a drone acting in the real world is constantly surprised by things it could not see coming. After a surprise, the useful question is no longer what was expected, but what would have happened had it acted differently in that same situation. You need that answer to debug a failure, to tell a bad decision from bad luck, or to decide what to do on the next attempt, and prediction alone does not provide it."

The researchers initial attempts to address the issue involved adding a learned component to the world model that infers whatever hidden disturbance (e.g. the current in the boat scenario) affected the anticipated outcome. But that approach was too fragile.

"Trying to understand why led to the theory," explained Balestriero. "Learning the disturbance from ordinary data is not just hard, it is impossible in general: the hidden noise can be relabeled differently for each action without changing a single prediction, so the data cannot tell you which labeling is the right one. The missing piece has to come from outside the data. For physical systems, it comes from the fact that forces add and that their interaction builds up slowly in time. Once you accept that, the learned disturbance model becomes unnecessary: the gap between what happened and what was predicted already carries the information you need, and you carry it over to the other action."

Balestriero said that control engineers have been implementing corrections of this sort for decades, to tune hand-built models.

"What was missing was why the same correction is justified for learned world models that see the world through images, what can and cannot be recovered without paired data, and where it breaks," he said. "The paper answers these questions by connecting causal inference, control and world models. The title comes from Leibniz's law of continuity, natura non facit saltus, 'nature makes no leaps,' which is precisely the property that makes all of this work."

The researchers' paper was provided to The Register prior to its release on ArXiv. It is expected to be released this week. ®
articles.summary: Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave.

articles.title: Microsoft takes three decades to make Sticky Keys less sticky
articles.text:
Windows testers are getting a new option in the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs – one to banish the pop-ups without needing to venture deep into Settings.

It's only taken several decades for Microsoft to put the off switch where the interruption actually happens. The accessibility features themselves are useful, though triggering their activation prompts by accident is another matter.

Once enabled, Sticky Keys let users press modifier keys (such as Control) one at a time instead of holding them down together. For example, rather than holding Control and pressing C to copy, a user can press and release Control, then press C. Filter Keys, meanwhile, ignores brief or repeated keystrokes and adjusts the keyboard's repeat behavior.

However, the dialogs are of little use to people who don't need the features, and they can pop up at the most inconvenient moments. Tap Shift five times, and you'll see what we mean: Windows chimes and shows a dialog asking whether you'd like to turn on Sticky Keys. Dismiss it, hit Shift five times, and there it is again.

Or hold down the right Shift key for eight seconds to be treated to the Filter Keys pop-up.

You can stop this behavior elsewhere in the system, but it requires a trek through Windows settings. The change, introduced in the Experimental Windows Insider Build 26340.9882, adds an option to the Sticky Keys or Filter Keys dialogs to dismiss the prompts permanently.

It's a small change, but one that should spare users an irritating interruption. Better late than never – even if "never ask me again" has taken roughly three decades to reach the dialog.

Former Microsoft engineer Charles Opperman said he wrote the dialog in early 1995 "after @bradsilverberg kids kept activating StickeyKeys [sic] while playing Space Cadet pinball."

Opperman added that a link to Settings was added in Windows 98 or what would become Windows 2000, and a checkbox was considered even then, but it wasn't deemed a priority. Users could turn off the prompt via settings. Now the option is front and center.

The option is also rolling out in the Windows Insider Beta channel, although Microsoft has not announced a general release date. ®

articles.title: Far-Right Group Targets Seattle Diwali Celebration With Provocative Placards
articles.text:
Far-right activists led by Jake Lang stormed Diwali celebrations in Seattle, carrying racist placards, an act that was swiftly condemned by US lawmakers and community leaders.
Lang and fellow activist Thomas Allen waved the American flag and carried placards with slogans “Deport All Dot Heads” and “Stop Hindu Replacement of Christians” in front of a stage at the Seattle Centre Armoury, where a dance performance was underway on Saturday.
Videos of the storming of the Diwali celebrations in Seattle went viral on social media. A large number of families and children were in attendance at the event.
The disruption by the far-right activists came a day after Trump lit the traditional diya at the Oval Office and Washington Governor Bob Ferguson joined the Diwali celebrations at the Indian Consulate General in Seattle.
The activists were soon escorted out of the Diwali celebrations, which were part of Seattle Centre Festival, a series of 25 free cultural festivals that collectively draw about 400,000 visitors annually.
Lang is associated with an organisation, ‘White Replacement,’ and was among the attackers of the US Capitol on January 6, 2021. He served a four-year jail term and was later pardoned by US President Donald Trump on the first day of his second presidency in 2025.
He said Hindu-Americans flipped Texas in favour of Democrats and claimed that recent US midterm elections were “rigged”. Lang also called for a demonstration at the US Capitol on January 3.
US lawmakers Pramila Jayapal and Raja Krishnamoorthi condemned the incident, saying such hate has no place in the US.
“I am beyond disgusted by this vile and racist display. Diwali is an important holiday and our community should feel safe to celebrate it. This hateful display has no place in our city or this country,” Jayapal, the Congresswoman from Washington, said in a post on X.
“Let’s proudly light a lamp today for Diwali, but resolve that we have to stamp out this hate directed toward Hindus and anyone,” Krishnamoorthi said.
Former White House advisor Ajay Jain Bhutoria said the actions of Lang and Allen were absolutely disgusting.
“Targeting Hindu Americans and Indian immigrants with racial slurs and conspiracy rhetoric has no place in this country. We stand against this racism and for the right of every American to celebrate their heritage freely,” Bhutoria said in a post on X.
“We condemn such actions and advise community members to stay vigilant while celebrating Diwali, as these activists have announced plans to disrupt other celebrations,” Coalition of Hindus of North America (CoHNA) said in a post on X.
Sunita Vishwanath, co-founder of Hindus for Human Rights, said anti-immigrant sentiment has taken the form of anti-Hindu hatred extreme enough for Christian xenophobes to “storm” a Diwali celebration in Seattle with signs like ‘Deport all Dotheads,’ a derogatory racial slur directed at people of South Asian descent — particularly Hindus — referencing the traditional forehead bindi or tilak.
“This is as heartbreaking as the Hindutva mobs that harass Christians in India on Christmas, forcing church congregations to say ‘Jai Shri Ram’ at the threat of violence,” Vishwanath said in a post on X.
“If we are appalled by this hateful and threatening behaviour of right-wing Christians towards Hindus, we must be equally appalled by the hate and violence that Indian Christians suffer at the hands of right-wing Hindus,” she said.
“We urge the Hindu community to stay vigilant and report any suspicious or hateful activity to local law enforcement,” advocacy group HinduPACT said in a post on X.

articles.title: Black Bunny: The F-14 Tomcat’s Rare All-Black Livery
articles.text:
Well known for its distinctive variable swept wing design, twin engines and interception range, the Tomcat has also been a few of the most unique aircraft used by the US Navy due to its unique fully black paint job and the famous white Playboy Bunny tail.
The Black Bunny aircraft were used by the US Navy’s test and evaluation unit, VX-4 (officially known as the Evaluators). However the tradition started with the McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II, with VX-4 painting it black and adding a bunny decal, the aircraft was know as Vandy 1 (based on the radio call sign used by the squadron, Vanderbilt) in 1969.
The Playboy Bunny caught the attention of Playboy Enterprises who contacted the squadron about the unauthorised use of the decal. Eventually the company allowed the Navy to use the decal as long as they used an official stencilling from the company. When the F-14A Tomcat was added to the unit, they continued the tradition. Two F-14A’s were painted black with a bunny decal in 1985. Initially the aircraft were painted with a water based paint, however around 1990 the Tomcats were permanently painted.
These were not an operational aircraft from the fleet, using a unique combat paint job, but were part of a unique test and evaluation unit. They looked stunning with their black paint, large twin tail and variable wings. They were often seen at air shows and events around Naval Air Station Point Mugu, California.
In September 1994 VX-4 and VX-5 (the Navy’s evaluation unit based at China Lake) merged into VX-9 (known as the Vampires).
The final F-14 ever built, the F-14D with Bureau Number 164604 became part of the Black Bunny tradition. It arrived at Point Mugu in September 1994 fully painted black, however it had the VX-9 decal. It had the bunny decal added back onto it for its final flights. On the 26th June 2004 the Tomcat flew from Point Mugu to Naval Air Station Oceana, Virginia. It is now a memorial aircraft and does not have the original Black Bunny paint.
The F-14 continued to be used by the US Navy until 2006 when it was retired, however the Black Bunny aircraft are now part of aviation history.

articles.title: NASA keeps its PROMISE to raid Mars testbeds for parts
articles.text:
NASA is moving ahead with its plan to repurpose a Mars rover engineering model as a lunar trundlebot for less than $400 million.

The robot, dubbed PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), is a cut-and-shut of engineering test articles used for the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers, currently rolling around the Red Planet.

During a weekend briefing, NASA outlined the plan for PROMISE: to land the robot on the lunar surface by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. PROMISE will be preceded by NASA's VIPER trundlebot, which is expected to survive only 100 days on the Moon's surface. PROMISE will carry copies of VIPER's science instruments, including a drill capable of boring 1 meter into the lunar regolith.

Power will come from a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) left over from the Cassini mission. NASA acknowledged the fuel was processed some time ago – the Cassini mission to Saturn was launched in 1997 – but anticipates there will be plenty of heat and power for PROMISE's components.

Blue Origin is to deposit the rover on the Moon. NASA awarded the company a $94 million base contract, "with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole."

The figures make it difficult to ascertain the exact cost of the PROMISE mission. However, during the briefing, NASA said it had "a pretty firm agreement with JPL to basically deliver the rover to the surface under $400 million." The $400 million includes the lander, which will be Blue Origin's Mark 1.

Earlier this year, The Planetary Society's chief of space policy, Casey Drier, estimated that the mission (including repurposing the hardware developed for Mars and landing it on the Moon) would cost at least $723 million. At the time, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said: "if PROMISE costs even 20 percent of your low-end estimate, we simply will not fly it."

Assuming Isaacman was only talking about the rover, Drier's figure drops to $489 million without launch and landing costs. 20 percent of that is… not going to be enough.

That also doesn't account for the impact of taking away the hardware built for the Mars program. During the briefing, NASA said it was "pretty comfortable" with how the Mars rovers were going and so was happy about repurposing the hardware or, as one speaker put it, "can we give it a new paint job?"

A source told The Register that morale at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) was not high at present. Raiding successful programs to fulfill the administration's whims is unlikely to have improved the mood of engineers.

Still. Another trundlebot on the Moon. Far better than using that spare RTG for yet another deep space mission, right? ®

articles.title: Hold up — I had a great time talking to the RIAA guy
articles.text:
Today, I’m talking with Mitch Glazier, who is CEO and chairman of the RIAA.

This conversation was a real full-circle moment for me: I was in college when Napster hit, and the RIAA became everyone’s villain for suing kids for downloading music. That was when I decided to go be a copyright lawyer, which set the rest of my career in motion — and Mitch was in the background as a young lawyer at the RIAA working on those cases. So part of me was very deeply, very genuinely surprised to discover just how much fun I had talking to Mitch.

That’s because here in 2026, Mitch, the RIAA, the record labels, the artists, and ordinary people are all pretty unhappy with the big AI companies in the same way, for training on everyone’s work without permission and flooding our feeds with slop.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Everyone is mad about it! And since the RIAA is both the group that lobbies for changes to the law and also the group that files lawsuits about things that affect record labels and distributors, Mitch is a pretty busy guy these days. We got deep into the legal complexity of things like AI deepfakes, how banning them might affect other kinds of expression, and how the AI detection and labeling systems that we all seem to want might actually work in practice — especially if big platforms like Spotify and YouTube don’t get on board.

I just want to get right into it. This conversation is a real ride through how AI, the law, art, and commerce might all intersect. I think you’re going to be able to tell, Mitch and I had a lot of fun talking about it.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: RIAA CEO Mitch Glazier. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Mitch Glazier, you’re the chairman and CEO of the Recording Industry Association of America, which people know as the RIAA. Welcome to Decoder.

Thank you. Thank you, Nilay. I’m excited to be here.

I am very excited to talk to you. I have to tell you, this is a very full-circle moment for me. My entire career got on track when I was in college. Napster came out, my university banned Napster from the school network, and I decided right then I was going to go be a copyright lawyer. And then I was a copyright lawyer, and I defended kids who got sued for using Kazaa. I was not good at that job. It was not fulfilling. And I became a journalist because I could write about copyright law on the iPod. So talking to you is about as full circle as it gets for me. Thank you for being on the show.

Good. Well then, I’m no longer sorry for the policies that we forced your school to implement because it made you a copyright lawyer. So the world benefited at the end of the day. It had some silver linings to it.

When I first started at the RIAA, Napster was obviously the big issue. Nobody had seen anything like it before. The last technological change had really been CDs. I mean, it had been a long time, a much more gradual change and much less abrupt. So they decided it’d be a good idea, since I was youngish at the time, to make me go to college campuses, go to auditoriums, and convince these college students that they shouldn’t use peer-to-peer technology.

Wait, wait, wait. I imagine when you said that, it was more like a 21 Jump Street situation, where you were posing in the dining hall being like, “We should pay for it.” Were you giving presentations?

Yes, it was horrible. Everybody had these anti-RIAA t-shirts on. I remember one time I followed Chuck D, who was there promoting peer-to-peer. And I didn’t know what to do, and I knew I was going to get booed. So I took a garbage bag, put it over my head, and I walked out onto the stage, thinking they were going to throw tomatoes at me; I might as well make light of it.

But I have to say, even though it was a very tough time, some of the conversations that we had with students at that time were some of the best conversations I’ve ever had — even now with AI — about the change in technologies, things being fan-driven, and the disconnect that can occur sometimes between an industry and the people who are out there driving change in the industry. So it was actually a good experience in the end, but it certainly did not feel like it at the time.

It didn’t feel like it at the time for me. Thank you for saying the butterfly effect is real. But it was heated. It was hot.

One of the things that has really occurred to me as I get older, and AI exists, and I see the platforms taking so much of the economic value out of art, is that my opinions about intellectual property enforcement have changed. It feels like I’m just giving up all of the ideals that I had when I was a kid about the internet, that open access to information was good, that… There was that meme ages ago: everything is a remix, and we should all build on each other’s art as much as we want because that will push the culture forward. I am still very idealistic about that. And I definitely did not think the recording industry suing kids was the appropriate way to protect the intellectual property of artists back then.

But here we are in the age of AI, and it feels like no one is making enough money for making art except the world’s biggest artists — who are all also tech investors now in some way — and the tech platforms that collect fractions of pennies from everything and are doing data center build-outs or whatever it is. And that just existential dynamic for me is where I wanted to start.

I want to talk about how the RIAA works and all the Decoder questions, but I was just thinking about what I really wanted to ask you, and it comes down to this: we have to protect the work, but there’s some balance in overprotecting the work that makes it harder for people to make new things. And my own journey with the RIAA is a reconsideration of that as more and more things get taken.

Where have you landed? You’ve been there for more than 20 years. How are you feeling about that balance?

Yeah, so the word balance is the right one, and it’s not an easy one. It’s one of those things where, over time, a barrier pops up here and then you kind of pivot, and then a barrier pops up here and you kind of pivot, and you sort of land in a zone that feels right because the responses that you’re getting, both from the creative community and from fans, start to line up. And I think in AI, they are lining up much more closely than they did during previous years of disruption.

Some of it has been because of the democratization of the industry, where the gatekeeping roles have changed, where the partnerships between those who partner and invest with artists and the artists themselves have changed. In a world where artists and label services, like à la carte services, are a bigger part of revenue, in an area where catalog, forever exploitation, and new investors in the industry have come in, the landscape is much wider now. And it’s not like there are just two types of big actors controlling or sharing in all of the money.

Now there are dozens of different types of folks meeting artists in different places where they are and meeting fans in different places where they are. And so it feels to me like this disruption, which is huge, and I hope we talk about it… The good news is, unlike Napster, I don’t feel like we are facing it at odds, which is kind of what it felt like back then. Now it feels like we’re not in the same place, but we’re kind of rowing in the same general direction, which is that everybody understands that art and commerce have always had tension, and there’s always going to have to be a balance. But authenticity and that connection between a human being artist and a fan, the preservation of that seems to be paramount in everything that we’re doing, whether you’re investing, listening, or performing.

And to me, we’re not fighting in this space anymore between just a business model or an investment. We are now fighting to keep the art as human and the connection between an artist and a fan preserved and alive. And that to me just seems like a much larger purpose, I guess. So it feels very different to me. It feels like a good bookend.

Like you, I started my career with Napster, but I was on the other side, learned a ton as a young lawyer, and now on the other side, we have AI, and comparing the two is so wild. I mean, the polls during Napster were like fans over here, and creators kind of hiding a little bit, and the companies over here. And now it’s like AI’s over here, and we’re all together on the other side.

Yeah. I mean, again, I cannot emphasize this enough: I was a bad lawyer, and I should not have been doing that job.

[Laughs] I doubt that.

I was not good at it. I really wasn’t. And what I remember from that time was that it was college kids; their universities would turn over their IP addresses, and they would get their little lawsuit. We would tell them, “We’re going to go to the district court in Chicago; you’re going to settle for $5,000, because that’s what the RIAA is running this program at. It’s a $5,000 settlement to break even on the cost and to deter you, and then you’re going to go work at the pizza place for a semester, pay your bill, and move on.” And I thought, this can’t be accomplishing a goal. The thing I’m doing right now is nothing. And maybe that’s why I felt like I was a horrible lawyer. Maybe that’s why I got out of it. But what you’re describing is the poles there, where there was no pushback on, well, these kids just love music. The thing they love is just music, and now they can get it, and they have it. They weren’t thinking about the business model of CDs.

That’s what Napster fundamentally disrupted. There was a scarce physical object that you could go pay $15 for, and if Metallica sold enough of those, their plane would get bigger, and everyone could kind of see that. And, “I’m listening to a lot of this music, and it should make you rich,” was nowhere close to reality. We’ve built those models now. We have built Spotify and Apple Music and all the subscription models. I want to talk about YouTube quite a bit, actually, where you can listen to a lot of music and some people will get rich, but a middle class of artists may just be totally hollowed out.
