So they kind of acknowledge upfront this could be a high cost of doing business going forward, and yet they’re going to have a spectacular IPO despite those risks. This means that they’re willing to bear them, and they’re also willing to accept the cost if and when that comes and it is secured.

Actually, I have a different view on that, and it’s related to the beginning of our conversation. I think you gave a quote to the Los Angeles Times where you said being the RIAA is more fun now because the consumers are on your side fighting the AI giants instead of you fighting consumers. I get that. The valence of the RIAA and the culture may have changed. I’m sure we’ll get some people in our comments saying it hasn’t, but in general, it’s changed, right? You’re on the side of the artist fighting the giants.

Google won all of those cases about fair use when it was a baby, right? And they had slides in the office, and they were a startup, and no judge had ever used the internet before, and they’re like, “I love YouTube!” And Viacom, you’re posting your videos on YouTube because your people love YouTube, and you know the audience is there. There was something very happy about the tech industry at that time. Google, as a company, was a hero.

I think these companies are villains now. But truly, and if you look at the polling, they are not beloved. AI is not beloved, particularly with young people. The idea that AI is theft is held by young people. That gives you an opportunity to actually turn the screws harder, to say maybe you shouldn’t bear these risks. Maybe the artists should be the ones getting rich, not the AI companies. Are you putting that into policy, or are you just trying to negotiate to an outcome?

No, we’re putting it into policy. Everything is an arc, as you know, but in the beginning of a disruption, you try to put into policy the basic rights that are going to allow the creators to control their creation, to charge what they want for their creation, and to develop the licensing deals that they feel they want to develop. And it’s gotten to be even bigger now than in the Napster days because back then, as you said, the transition was from CDs. So the artist only made money in those days during a few months after release, and then some CDs still sold for years afterwards, but a lot of them ended up in warehouses, and you kind of had this small window.

The streaming revolution allows “exploitation,” not in the negative sense, but in the positive sense. It allows it to last forever. That’s why you have all these new investors coming into the music community because it’s a little bit more like a commodity now. That’s why Goldman Sachs is buying catalogs. That’s why all of these new companies are coming in, and they’re buying catalogs of music because music’s evergreen. It’s water. People are going to love it forever.

And as an artist, you now have an opportunity you never had in the past. It’s not just to make this chunk on the wholesale cost of CDs within a certain month period; it’s, “Hey, now that I’ve built up this following and people might love these songs 20 years from now, guess what? I can now sell my catalog for a large amount of money to an investor in the future.”

I just want to hit pause here and say that the baby punk rocker in me is… We could do another full hour on artists who now have the opportunity to sell their catalog to Goldman Sachs. It’s another hour. I know it’s there.

Listen, we are all 20-something at some time, and then we’re 50-something at another time. Everybody wants to take care of their grandkids at some point.

But this is an opportunity that they have now that they didn’t have before. And so I think that this disruption… I think there’s more skin in the game for the actual creator than there was in the past when the revenue was more bifurcated or trifurcated. Nobody on the creative side of the equation thinks that it’s right that Suno will be making all the money from all of the music that has been created in the past, and that substitutional effect is going to deprive the artist or any of their partners.

If the artist is in the middle of the sun and you’ve got all the folks around them from performing rights organizations, to record companies, to publishers, to managers, to producers, to agents, et cetera, they’re all sort of partners in a piece of that larger puzzle. And now the artist has more skin in the game than they ever had before, which is another reason why I think we’re sort of rowing together a little bit longer.

There are other outcomes here. I think it’s Warner that’s partnered with Suno; they made a model on Warner’s music so they don’t run into these issues. If that proliferates, then you don’t get to sue the AI music companies because they made their models with licensed music, but you’ll face a supply problem on platforms like Spotify where you can suddenly flood the platforms with music.

Your solution there, at least as I understand this conversation, is labeling. You’re going to put labels on the AI stuff so the fans can make a market decision, and the bet is the fans will choose humans. Is there another solution to the glut of supply?

Yeah. I think an immediate solution for the marketplace for now is labeling. But I also think that these licensing agreements matter. I’m not privy to the licensing agreements that exist with Suno or any other AI company because I represent competitors, so they would never tell me. But I would imagine that it’s about dilution: where you don’t want to put artists’ music at risk on streaming platforms, because 90 percent of what they’re competing with is AI slop, if I could use that term. The licensing agreement gives you the leverage and the ability, if your rights are secured, to say, “I’m not going to let you download all this stuff.”

I mean, it’s rumored that in the Udio agreement, a walled garden had to be built so that fans could make music within the network on their own Spotify-like app. It wouldn’t discourage them from also having Spotify or Apple; it increases the revenue for everybody, but we’re not going to allow you to download from this platform and dilute that platform.

I don’t know if that’ll work. That seems to be one model. It could be that the terms with Suno had a limit on it or considered supply. I’m not a business person; I’m a policy person. But I think that there are plenty of ways, if the rights are secured, that through licensing arrangements and agreements, creators could then have the leverage to affect the supply so as not to cannibalize the work that they have on other platforms.

Well, I think the policy problem of supply is that it will affect the business somehow. We should talk about Spotify for a minute. It’s amazing that we haven’t spent more time talking about Spotify.

I know!

I think the model companies are not going to listen. You can see what they are doing. They are gluttonous for data, and they think that they can outrun the consequences. We’ll see what happens there. Spotify is not training a model. Spotify is just distributing music. That’s the thing that they’re doing; they’re a pure-play business in that way, and they have a lot of incentives for AI music to replace the music they have to otherwise pay for on that platform. They have a lot of incentives for white noise and fake streams in history to do these things, and they’ve gotten in trouble for some of it. This is a real thing that happens on this platform. Are they going to participate in a labeling scheme and say, “This is AI music?”

I think so, because as much as they have an economic incentive to lower their costs, their biggest economic incentive is to keep fans paying $9.99, $12.99, $15.99 per month. And so if fans feel duped, if you are putting —

Is that proven out in the market? I’m actually very curious about this.

Yes.

You’re saying there’s AI slop on Spotify now, or when you search for Taylor Swift, you get a bunch of weird Taylor Swift soundalikes, which is an experience everyone has on Spotify. It hasn’t churned those fans yet. There’s not some exodus to Tidal or Apple Music. Spotify is still dominant in its way.

Right. I think they’re walking down the road slowly, probably a little too slowly. I’m trying to see if they can do just enough to keep those two things in balance. Right now, for example, Spotify is saying, “We will only disclose or label a recording as AI in the credits.” Well, how many people look at the credits? I wish more people looked at the credits; they would discover producers and songwriters and other awesome folks who have contributed to the recording — but they don’t.

They need to do it at the track level. They’re not there yet. But they are disclosing AI personas that are made, because that’s sort of the highest on the dupe scale. And then under that, they’re looking at the fact that 90 percent of the recordings available on Spotify get 10 percent of the revenue, and 10 percent of the content gets 90 percent of the revenue. It’s because most of what’s on there gets less than 10 listens, or less than a hundred listens, and all of this slop is just going on, which means storage costs and all sorts of other things that they have to think about.

So I think that they will go as far down the road as fans will demand, as their users will demand. I think we’ll get to a point where people get these recommendations in their algorithm. “If you like this song, you’ll also like this one.” And when you listen to it, it turns out it was AI, you didn’t know it was AI, and you’ll feel deceived. That’s when they’ve got a giant problem because they’re responsible for that recommendation. They’re the ones that fed that to you. And we do have lots of consumer research out there showing that subscribers, just like all consumers, want to feel like nobody’s pulling the wool over their eyes.

But is there an actual market pressure? I can think of all kinds of times fans have revolted against Spotify. I love the band Stars, and every now and again they’ll tweet, “We didn’t make any money on this song on Spotify.” And everyone tweets at Spotify, and they’re mad. Spotify’s not paying artists any more money. Is there an actual market pressure that will make this labeling happen, or is it policy pressure?

It’s both. It’s a combination, because there are already laws in other countries that are mandating labels. And once a market like the EU or the US — that’s such a big market — or the UK or China, once they demand labeling on a global system, it’s actually cheaper to do it all around the world than it is to just geo-block it in one country.

This is the California car emission model of regulation, right?

It’s amazing what California can do because these companies are headquartered there. I mean not Spotify, but Apple and Google and others. And so the transparency law in California is the reason why Suno has to, as of August, put a watermark saying, “This is AI-generated” that’s machine-readable. One state, but they’re doing it all over the world because that’s what… So it’s a combination of policy, which obviously we are very directly engaged in, and competition. I predict that what Apple decides to do that is more fan-friendly will drive Spotify, and vice versa.

There’s not that much churn between them, but if there’s some sort of perception that you’re being more subscriber-friendly than somebody else, that tends to drive results. It does the same on the privacy issue, for example, where there’s no law on it, but now companies are competing to say, “We’re the private browser. Apple, we protect your privacy.”

One company says that. Let me ask you this. I’ve only got a few minutes left, and I want to take one turn at the end to talk about how you measure for platinum certification, because that’s also up in the air.

But let me just ask you one more question here on labeling. We have spent a lot of time at The Verge covering labels for images and media. There are all these standards that exist. I have one poor reporter, her name is Jess Weatherbed, and she has been forced to learn everything about the C2PA standard and content, SynthID, and all these things.

I’m so sorry. It’s really important, though.

They’re very important, and we spend a lot of time covering them because they have to work. And they have to work in a number of different places in the chain, right? They have to work in the camera, in Photoshop, on Twitter, and everyone has to agree. If Elon Musk does not want SynthID to show up on his platform, it doesn’t matter if it worked in the camera. This is a big chain.

It seems harder in music, much harder because a bunch of bedroom DJs are probably not going to participate in your technical scheme for labeling when they upload to DistroKid. An artist getting a beat from a producer over iMessage — who knows if that metadata will survive. You might have to watermark the sound files themselves in some deep intrinsic way, and that can get you into all kinds of trouble because now you’re screwing with the audio files at the software level and artists don’t like that. How do you make labeling work at all?

Yeah, you’re hitting on our daily meetings. So I mean, there are the international organizations like DDEX, for example, that can help align fields and stuff like that. C2PA, which can give you a model for provenance. But at the end of the day, it has to be the platforms and the distributors that are willing to do it. Because when it comes to generative AI, the record labels are not tagging and putting generative AI up on Spotify. That’s out of the DIY world.

That’s somebody going to a music generator, downloading it, and putting it up through DistroKid. So your gateway is DistroKid, TuneCore. It’s the distributors. Are they using AI detection technology to determine that it’s fully generated? You might not be able to use AI detection technology to say your song is five percent of this or use it for attribution yet, but you can definitely use it to say this is fully generated AI. And if so, are they willing to tag it so that it works with Apple and Spotify’s platform?

Then, on the platforms themselves, this is sort of like the parental advisory program; it might be voluntary, and everybody might have a little bit of a different way of implementing it, but fans are pretty clear. When something’s labeled as parental advisory, which probably just draws more young people to listen to it —

It did to me.

But when it’s labeled as parental advisory, people kind of get it. They know. It’s become sort of a culturally known thing. I think labeling for fully generated AI can definitely get there, but the distributors have to be willing to play. It can’t just be the platforms because if it doesn’t go downstream, they’re going to go in different directions. And already, Deezer’s going in one direction, Apple’s going in another direction, Spotify’s going in another direction. To me, the fully generated problem, which is a DIY problem, is a distributor problem. And we have to provide incentives to the distributors to get them to take responsibility and play ball.

Do you think that technology exists to support the policy there? You need a technology that can detect AI-generated media. I’m not sure that any of that exists or works well.

I think it exists and works well for fully generated AI music. We also do a lot of testing at the RIAA. That’s another thing that our tech team does. And then we disclose the results back to the folks who gave it to us. We won’t disclose it to anybody else, but if you want to know what our test says about your technology, we’ll tell you.

And I think when it comes to fully generated AI, there’s plenty of detection technologies out there that do a really good job. Once you get below that, time will make it better. So I don’t know that we could get into a lot of gradations right now. Deezer, very successfully, on a platform level, uses AI detection technology and then labels what it detects as fully generated AI, and it’s got a very low false positive rate.

I want to end by talking about the certifications for platinum records and so on. It’s an important part of what you do. All the artists want their little records on their wall. It’s amazing that it’s still records. One of our jokes at The Verge is also that no one knows how to count anything, that Nielsen ratings — I should probably disclose, we are now part of the company that owns Luminate, which powers the Billboard charts.

The Billboard charts and their methodology are always in flux. Actually, I think as of this year, they’re in a fight with YouTube. YouTube does not want to be counted on the Billboard charts because some methodologies are… Counting is very political.

It is.

You literally give awards for counting to a big number. That is in flux as artists gain more attention on TikTok. And I have probably heard that whole Nicole Kidman song, in fragments on TikTok. I’ve never listened to the whole thing all the way through, and I’m certainly never going to buy a copy of it. Again, all in flux, and then somewhere in there is a bunch of AI remixes, and now I’ve listened to “Pop Star” by Drake 10,000 times because Darth Vader is singing it to me.

How are you thinking about that methodology, as to who’s creating what? AI is in the mix, and we’re listening to more and more fragments to discover songs on social platforms than anything else.

I swear to God, you are in my daily meetings.

Can I just tell you? I’m happy to hear that. I drive The Verge team crazy because I’m like, the music industry is the future always. And they’re like, no one wants to listen to that. So thank you for indulging me. I appreciate you.

I mean, you have your finger on the pulse. This is exactly the type of stuff we’re thinking of. So right now we’re still in the world of 1500 streams equaling one unit, and what used to be the sale of a CD. Now it’s obviously singles-based more than albums-based, although we still do certify albums. And if you look at the chart eligibility program that is now being implemented outside of Billboard and OCC, in other places of the world, they have made rules to say, unless it’s substantially human, we are not going to allow it to be eligible for the chart because you’re literally taking the place of a human artist on number 49. Billboard, so far, will allow it, but they’ll label it.

We haven’t, because we certify albums that were released by record companies. We have yet to run into the issue of the AI slop or the machine-created piece. But as we get more into assistive AI, as creators start to use AI more, and you look at the chart eligibility of substantially human, does a stream as part of that 1500 mean that it still has to be a human stream? Yes, I’m sure that we will come down on that side.

But what does substantially human mean? I think over time that might change. It might be different three years from now than it is today. But at the core, it’s got to be in the control of the creator. And some people would argue that putting nine words into a music generator is an act of creation.

Oh, they will. They’re going to. Yeah.

And that they are a creator, and therefore it’s the same thing. It’s not the same thing. Not saying that craft doesn’t change over time, and that in songwriting it’s also different than in producing and creating a recording. Using AI in the songwriting process may look very different than it does in the recording process, so we have to think about that too. But as far as gold and platinum go, we are still in the reliably safe zone of being able to know with a great deal of certainty exactly what we’re doing. I think the evolution over time is going to be in how creators use AI more than it will need to be in something that’s fully machine-readable or machine-created.

Well, Mitch, you’ve given us so much time. As you can tell, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed this conversation. I could keep going for hours and hours now.

Me too. I mean, honestly, this has been awesome. You freaked me out a little bit because you… It’s so great to see, though, because the stuff that you’re focused on is exactly what we are trying to grapple with every single day. And I think where we’ve come to is that we can’t pretend that there are easy answers. We can’t just react sort of in a knee-jerk way. We’ve got to try to figure out a path forward that’s going to allow the industry to change and grow. This industry’s adapted more times than any other industry in the history of our country. I mean, nobody goes from wax cylinders to AI in a hundred years. Can you imagine asking Boeing to make cars? So, a very adaptable industry.

I agree with you that we’re ahead of the game and that we are the future. We’re sort of living it. And the lessons that we learned from the music industry, we can apply to a lot of other things. So this has been awesome.

Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Really appreciate it.

You got it. Take care.

articles.title: Bangladesh Return? Sheikh Hasina Reportedly Seeks New Passport
articles.text:
Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina requested on Monday a new passport and identity card so she can return from self-imposed exile in India, according to a letter seen by Reuters, her first such communication since fleeing in 2024.
The request marks the clearest step by Hasina to act on her plan to return to Bangladesh in December, more than two years after a deadly uprising ended her long rule, raising the prospect of fresh political and legal tensions in a country where her party is now banned.
She has told Reuters she plans to return to surrender before a court, and her aides said on Monday the date would be announced once various formalities were completed. Bangladesh’s war-crimes court sentenced her to death in November last year in her absence for ordering a deadly crackdown on the student-led uprising, though she has denied the charges from exile.
“In view of the reported revocation of her existing Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card (NID) by the Interim Government and other authorities, I respectfully request that you take the necessary steps to issue a new Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card for our client,” Hasina’s lawyers at London-based Matrix Chambers wrote to Preeti Rahman, acting high commissioner at Bangladesh’s embassy in Delhi.
The letter asked for the applications to be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of her Bangladeshi nationality and in accordance with “obligations arising under international human rights instruments”. Rahman in Delhi and spokespeople for Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in Dhaka did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Hasina’s Awami League party was the country’s largest before it was banned following her fall. Many of her party colleagues have either been jailed or are in self-imposed exile in India or elsewhere. 
Having ruled Bangladesh for 20 years as prime minister across multiple terms, Hasina still enjoys support among sections of the population, and a return could sharpen political divisions as the government in Dhaka seeks to restore stability after more than two years of upheaval.
On the other hand, it could improve Bangladesh’s strained ties with India, which deteriorated sharply after New Delhi gave her refuge.

articles.title: F1 in Brazil: You’ve got to keep your tires alive
articles.text:
In sports, a “dead rubber” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. The people in charge hate this*—if you wrap up a title two-thirds of the way through a season, the viewers evaporate, as there’s nothing left at stake. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty.

A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. Take McLaren’s Lando Norris, who took the crown in 2025 after a nail-biting fight with his teammate Oscar Piastri and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Sadly for Lando, McLaren did not start this year in a position to win races, and even with several upgrades, the team has produced a car that is still very tricky to drive. But this weekend in Brazil, Norris demonstrated the form that earned him the number 1.

Rain on Saturday during qualifying helped jumble the usual running order. It was heavy enough that drivers used the wet weather tire with deep treads, which usually generates so much spray that visibility disappears and running has to be suspended. But with fewer cars on track in the later knockout qualifying sessions, this was not a problem for once. More disruption came from grid penalties for Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, both of whom needed to use extra power unit components outside of the season’s allowance.

Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session
articles.text:
Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking.

Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on.

Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release.

The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1.

There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident, tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another.

Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog.

The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata.

The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported earlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel.

Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release.

Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest.

And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

articles.title: Indian Navy Seeks Adversary Ship Silhouettes for Training
articles.text:
The Indian Navy has issued a tender to fabricate and install enemy ship silhouettes at the Officers Training Area of INS Dronacharya at Fort Kochi, Kerala for use in Warship Recognition exercises and Gun Drill training. The tender, GEM/2026/B/8232612, was issued on the GeM portal on November 3, 2026. It requires one lot of Enemy Ship Silhouette for use at the naval training facility. The goods need to be delivered to INS Dronacharya, Fort Kochi. The work needs to be completed within 180 days of signing the contract.
INS Dronacharya is the Indian Navy’s training facility for Gun Drill and Missile Warfare. The ship silhouettes will be used for training the navy on handling weapons, Gun Drill and other related activities. They will simulate enemy ships for training.
Ship recognition through silhouettes plays an important part in maritime training. Different superstructure layouts, masts, funnel positions and hull profiles can help identify different types of naval vessels.
Ship shaped silhouettes can be used for laying guns and rapid fire exercises.Technical specifications of the product including size, materials and installation requirements can be found within the attachments uploaded by the buyer. These include Scope of Work and Additional Terms & Conditions. This works tender requires only one lot. No EMD or performance Bank Guarantee is required.
The tender allows full flexibility on previous experience and turnover requirements for eligible Micro and Small Enterprises and recognised DPIIT startups. The OEM will require an average turnover of ₹1 lakh in the last 3 financial years. Other eligible bidders will require one year experience supplying similar products.
The bid requires a two packet evaluation. It will be awarded using a reverse auction method and the highest priced bidder will be excluded. Preference has been given to eligible MSE suppliers by the Navy. Up to 25% of the total quantity can be supplied with a preference of up to L1 + 15%.

articles.title: BrahMos-NG Draws Growing Attention in Turkish Media
articles.text:
The BrahMos-NG programme has received some attention in Türkiye’s defence media. There were a number of articles written in Turkish late October and early November 2026. However, much of this seems to be second-hand information from Indian reports.
Looking at 5 articles since May 2025 relating to the BrahMos-NG programme there seems to be increased interest in the missile’s testing schedule, aircraft integration and export potential. 3 of these articles were written in quick succession between each other.
Savunma.net wrote an article on 26 October regarding how the missile is likely to fit into the international aviation industry. The article noted the missile’s reduced size when compared to the current air-launched BrahMos-A variant and possible integration with various fighter aircraft.
Timeturk wrote a more general article on 24 October regarding the missile’s P-800 Oniks heritage, the Indo-Russian joint venture, it’s reported usage in Operation Sindoor and extending ranges. ULU Savunma also wrote articles about BrahMos-II and integration possibilities with fighter aircraft. However, the most notable thing was the reliance on Indian media. The 4 November article on Savunma.net included technical details which were also reported earlier in the day in Indian reports. These included aerodynamic coefficient calculations, thrust curve calculations, control surface design, guidance law design, seeker design and environment modelling.
The article also directly referenced IDRW in regards to the modifications required to integrate the original BrahMos-A onto the Su-30MKI.
Whilst it is not unusual to see foreign defence media citing specialised media in the country producing a certain weapon system, it should be understood that the reports are not actually independent confirmation of development milestones and technical performance.
There are also inconsistencies in the information provided. The October article mentions a Mach 3 speed whereas the November article mentions a speed of +3.5Mach. The May 2025 article from ULU Savunma mentions that the missile will be procured in a quantity of 400 over 5 years, although this should be treated with caution unless confirmed by an official procurement statement.
The reason for the interest is likely to be due to the missile’s potential export potential and it’s reported usage in combat. Being able to provide a smaller version of BrahMos would mean the missile would appeal to air forces with less room to fit the heavier BrahMos-A.
Operation Sindoor has been heavily referenced throughout the articles. The missile has reportedly performed well during this operation, which would be relevant for international marketing. However, this should be treated as individual claims rather than verified battle damage assessment.
Finally, Pakistan could also be a reason for the increased interest. Turkish defence media often covers developments impacting Pakistan and having BrahMos capabilities would have clear implications for air defence within the region. However, this is not confirmed from the articles.

India and Myanmar Conclude First-Ever Tri-Services HADR Exercise
articles.text:
The inaugural bilateral Tri-Services Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) Exercise ‘RAHAT MITRA’, conducted between the Defense Forces of India and Myanmar on 05 and 06 Nov 2026, concluded at Chennai. The two-day exercise brought together personnel from the Indian Navy, Indian Army and Indian Air Force, along with a delegation from the Myanmar Defense Forces, to enhance operational interoperability, improve coordination and facilitate the exchange of Best Practices in disaster response operations.
The exercise commenced with a focus on joint planning and familiarization with HADR capabilities. A Table-Top Exercise (TTX), based on a severe cyclone scenario, facilitated discussions on coordinated response mechanisms and joint disaster management protocols. The participating contingents also witnessed demonstrations of obstacle clearance and bridge-laying capabilities by the Indian Army and visited INS Sukanya to gain insights into the Indian Navy’s shipborne HADR capabilities.
On the second day, the participating contingents witnessed demonstrations of multi-domain HADR capabilities by the Indian Defense Forces, highlighting coordinated response mechanisms across maritime, land and air domains. INS Adyar and Communication Network Centre, Chennai, showcased shore-based disaster response arrangements and communication infrastructure supporting command and control during emergencies. Military Hospital, Chennai, demonstrated field medical triage and the coordinated management of disaster relief camps.
The Indian Navy’s Flood Relief Teams (FRT) demonstrated specialized equipment and capabilities for flood relief operations. Maritime Search and Rescue (SAR) capabilities were also showcased through coordinated maneuvers involving a Chetak helicopter and INS Bitra. The Indian Air Force demonstrated casualty evacuation capabilities, with Commodore Aung Niang Win and two officers of the Myanmar delegation onboard an IAF ALH during airborne operations.
Exercise ‘RAHAT MITRA’ provided an important platform for the Defense Forces of both countries to exchange operational experiences, share Best Practices and enhance mutual understanding in planning and executing HADR operations. The exercise also facilitated familiarization with each other’s capabilities and procedures, contributing to improved coordination during disaster response operations.
The successful culmination of the inaugural exercise reinforces the commitment of India and Myanmar to advancing bilateral defense cooperation and enhancing collective preparedness for disaster response. It also underscores the shared resolve of both nations to contribute to regional stability, maritime cooperation and effective HADR.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made 

—By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm

This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story.

Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests  

Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. 

The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. 

For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. 

Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate. 

—Matthew Ponsford

articles.title: VEDA Aeronautics Teases MALE UAV Design for India’s 87-Drone Programme
articles.text:
Delhi-based VEDA Aeronautics Private Limited has given a new look at what may be their design for their Medium Altitude Long Endurance (MALE) Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) to win India’s key 87 MALE drone acquisition programme. The aircraft can be seen in the company’s Diwali card and shows a long winged UAV with a nose-on view.
VEDA Aeronautics have previously confirmed they will enter the race to supply India’s MALE UAV requirement. This has become a hotly contested race between many Indian Defence companies. What makes this image interesting is that VEDA have not specified any detailed technical information about the aircraft.
The aircraft in the image appears to be a large UAV with a long straight wing design. It has a central fuselage with traditional landing gear. There is also what appears to be an electro optical turret underneath the nose. The dimensions of the aircraft suggest it would be suitable for long endurance missions but there is not enough detail in the image to determine how it is powered, what the dimensions are or what the final design will be.
India’s 87 aircraft MALE UAV requirement is a key acquisition with a value of over Rs 30,000 crore. It will give the Indian Armed Forces a new generation of UAVs capable of carrying out ISR missions.
This is being done through Indian companies who can offer a home grown solution or partner up with well known UAV manufacturers. This will help boost local manufacturing.
Around ten bids were received from public and private sector companies in India ahead of the deadline, according to reports from June 2026. Companies who have been named include Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, Tata Advanced Systems Limited, Larsen & Toubro, Adani Defence Systems, Solar Defence and Aerospace Limited and Raphe mPhibr.
VEDA entering the race means there are now more private sector companies entering the race. It had previously garnered some attention back in 2025 when details of their MALE UAV design were released. It was armed with a turboprop engine and had provisions for air-to-surface weapons.
However, it is not clear if this aircraft is the same design, an upgraded design or a completely different design. VEDA have not released any specs on the aircraft including endurance, service ceiling, payload, engine type or weapons.

articles.title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
articles.text:
As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.

Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”

Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.

“Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.

These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.

Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.”

articles.title: DRDO Awards Blockchain Security Project Under TDF Scheme
articles.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has awarded a new technology development project focused on blockchain security and auditing to IHUB NTIHAC Foundation at IIT Kanpur under its Technology Development Fund (TDF) scheme.
According to DRDO, the project titled “Security Analysis & Auditing of Blockchain” was awarded on 6 November 2026. DRDO’s Scientific Analysis Group (SAG) has been designated as the nodal laboratory for the project.
The proposed project is centred on security analysis and auditing, an important area for identifying vulnerabilities in blockchain-based systems and assessing their resilience against potential cyber threats.
The project has been awarded to M/s IHUB NTIHAC Foundation, an organisation associated with IIT Kanpur. Its selection under the TDF scheme reflects DRDO’s continued engagement with academic institutions and technology-focused organisations for developing capabilities relevant to national defence requirements.
Blockchain technology offers a distributed approach to recording and verifying information, but it is not inherently immune to cyberattacks. Vulnerabilities in smart contracts, access controls, consensus mechanisms and implementation can expose blockchain networks to manipulation or exploitation.
For defence-related applications, security auditing could be relevant to systems requiring tamper-resistant records, secure information exchange and trusted digital transactions. Any such application, however, would depend on the project’s eventual technical outcomes and DRDO’s specific requirements.

articles.title: New Democratic Congress will likely strip the gilding from Trump's Golden Dome
articles.text:
Two of the top lawmakers backing the Pentagon's Golden Dome missile defense shield are among the wave of Republicans leaving Congress in the coming Democratic takeover, raising questions about the future of President Donald Trump's signature second-term defense initiative.

The shakeup on Capitol Hill comes after military officials signaled in recent months that they might backpedal from one element Trump asked for in Golden Dome: the capability to shoot down missiles in their initial boost phase shortly after launch.

The Golden Dome has escaped serious congressional scrutiny since Trump announced the program in January 2025, one week into his second term in the White House. That lack of scrutiny will change as Democrats take responsibility for writing the Pentagon's budget, introduce limits on funding, and put forth bills to strip out Golden Dome's most controversial component and give the program a new name.
